proposal.root_problem: Refunds submitted through the refund process (P-REF) are failing outright at the payment system due to invalid IBAN format (5/5 sampled failures = FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, E-01), causing customers to repeatedly recontact support chasing never-completed refunds; support itself replies well within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA, E-02), so the backlog is driven by unresolved refund failures, not by slow support answer delivery as the initial request framed it.
proposal.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds (SH-SUP initial request).
symptoms: Stakeholder perceives customers waiting a long time for refund answers and requests a chatbot (CL-01).
Repeated customer contact with support generating a refund-related ticket backlog despite support replying within SLA (E-02).
Refunds failing outright with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT at the payment system (E-01).
causal_chain: Refunds submitted via the refund process (P-REF) are rejected by the payment system with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT due to invalid IBAN validation (E-01, F-01).
Rejected refunds never complete, so affected customers do not receive their expected refund.
Affected customers repeatedly contact support to chase the never-completed refund, generating tickets.
Support agents actually reply within SLA (median 2.0h vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets, E-02), so the repeated contact is not explained by slow answer delivery.

The resulting ticket backlog is perceived by the requesting stakeholder as a response-speed problem (CL-01/CL-02/E-03), prompting the chatbot request, which masks the underlying IBAN-validation defect.

assumptions.statement: The 900 tickets measured in E-02 substantially overlap with the refund-related tickets driving the stakeholder's complaint, making the SLA comparison relevant to the refund-wait issue.
The 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records returned by payment-db.refund_failures reflect an ongoing defect pattern relevant to the current backlog, not an isolated historical artifact.

proposal.summary: The stakeholder (SH-SUP) initially asked for a chatbot to stop customers waiting for refund answers (CL-01). Investigation (E-01, E-02) found instead that refunds are failing outright at the payment system due to an IBAN-format validation defect in process P-REF, and that support itself replies well within its SLA, so the backlog is driven by unresolved refund failures, not slow answers (PD-1 root_problem). The release delivers only the quantification of this failure population from payment-db (5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records, E-01/F-01) as scoped in solution_design SD-1 minimum_useful_scope and release_scope; the fix, reprocessing, and ticket-linkage correlation work are not released. The decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION because the DEFINE gate returned CONDITIONAL_PASS with a high-impact unknown deferred outside the released scope, several verification obligations remain open, and a tool outage blocks further action this session.
key_points: Original request was a chatbot for slow refund answers (CL-01, stakeholder SH-SUP), but evidence E-01 (payment-db.refund_failures: 5 of 5 sampled records FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT) and E-02 (ticket-db.response_times: median 2.0h reply vs 24h SLA across 900 tickets) support hypothesis H-REFUND-FAILURE-IBAN and reject H-SLOW-ANSWER-DELIVERY and H-REFUND-PROCESSING-DELAY.
The redefined root problem (PD-1): refunds fail outright on IBAN format validation in P-REF, driving repeated customer contact, while support response times are within SLA (E-01, E-02).

The DEFINE gate result was CONDITIONAL_PASS, deferring the critical unknown U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE (what fraction of tickets are actually caused by failed refunds) as VOB-U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE, which falls outside the release scope.

What was released: only the quantify_iban_failure_population action on DA-PAY, i.e. the count of 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records, per solution_design SD-1 release_scope and minimum_useful_scope; work item W-WI-1 is DONE.

Not released: fixing the IBAN validation defect in P-REF (SC-FIX-IBAN-FAILURES) and reprocessing the 5 failed refunds (SC-REPROCESS-EXISTING-FAILURES) are marked not feasible in contest time and remain as handoff items with no designated P-REF owner (VOB-R-4, OPEN, required before production).

Open verification obligations near the release: VOB-R-2 (does uncertainty about DA-PAY completeness mean the count of 5 understates true failures) is non-critical and intersects release scope; VOB-R-3 (whether DEGRADED bank-api settlement_status relates to the IBAN failures and blocks reprocessing) and VOB-R-4 are required before production, not before this release.

Multiple root-cause conflicts (C-1 through C-7) on assertion refund_wait.root_cause remain OPEN between the stakeholder claims CL-01 and CL-02 and the evidence E-01, E-02, E-03, though the evidence-based explanation is the one carried into the released problem definition.

The bank-api tool is DEGRADED with ACCESS_DENIED; a recovery_decision (seq 61) stopped retries as NOT_TRANSIENT with no fallback, which is why reprocessing-related work could not proceed this session.
limitations_explained: The quantified failure count of 5 (metric M-IBAN-FAILURE-COUNT) comes from a 5-record sample with an unknown total refund-attempt denominator, so no true failure rate can be computed yet.

There is an unresolved inconsistency in the data: the release limitations and VOB-R-2 treat DA-PAY completeness as UNKNOWN, implying the count of 5 could undercount the real failure population (unknown U-FAILURE-POPULATION-SIZE, OPEN), while the recorded data asset entry for DA-PAY lists completeness as COMPLETE; this discrepancy is unresolved and should be checked before the figure is used to report status.

No write or deploy tool was available this session, so the IBAN validation fix and refund reprocessing could not be executed and must be handed off, and no process owner for P-REF is currently recorded to receive that handoff (VOB-R-4, OPEN, required before production).

The bank-api tool is DEGRADED (ACCESS_DENIED on settlement_status) and whether this is related to the IBAN validation failures is unresolved (unknown U-BANK-API-DEGRADATION-RELATIO, VOB-R-3, OPEN), so it is uncertain whether refund reprocessing is even feasible once a fix exists.

The critical unknown of what fraction of the 900-ticket backlog is actually caused by failed refunds versus other causes such as lack of self-service visibility or a general ticket volume surge is deferred (VOB-U-TICKET-REFUND-LINKAGE, HIGH impact) and lies outside what was released, so the released IBAN count should not be read as proof of the ticket backlog's full cause or scale.
